plan.topic: Does tirzepatide make you tired? Fatigue in the Zepbound label (5%, 6% and 7% by dose vs 3% on placebo, pooled SURMOUNT-1 and -2) and common, checkable reasons
plan.angle: 08:00 calm 'honest uncertainty' body-worry Short, 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer. Open within 10 s: 'Feeling wiped out on tirzepatide? Fatigue is on the label, but it's uncommon: 5 to 7 percent across doses versus 3 percent on placebo in the trials.' Verify the figures and the pooled-trial population against the FDA label itself, not Healthline. One line: eating much less, low fluids or skipped protein can all leave you tired. That's 'can', not proven cause. Then what's worth checking with a clinician: how much you're eating and drinking, and whether blood tests make sense (iron and others). No supplement promises and no dosing. Red flag: dizziness or fainting, or vomiting with signs of dehydration, means contact your prescriber promptly. One GI line. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. Loop ending, no emoji, mix at 0.02 or lower.

package.title: Does Tirzepatide Cause Fatigue? What the Label Shows #shorts
package.description:
In two trials of adults with obesity or overweight, 5–7% reported fatigue across tirzepatide doses vs 3% on placebo, so most people didn't. Low food or fluid intake, anemia, or low blood sugar (if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea) are worth checking with a clinician.
Don't stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
Sources: Zepbound Prescribing Information (Lilly/FDA); NHS: Tiredness and fatigue.
#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #Zepbound #SideEffects

factcheck.summary: The science holds up and the Short is safe to publish once three small fixes are made. I checked the current US Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised Aug 28, 2026). Fatigue is listed at 5% on 5 mg, 6% on 10 mg and 7% on 15 mg, versus 3% on placebo. Those figures pool two 72-week placebo-controlled trials in adults with obesity or overweight: Study 1 had no type 2 diabetes, Study 2 had type 2 diabetes. The label's 'fatigue' also counts asthenia, lethargy and malaise. So '5–7% across the three doses vs 3% on placebo' and 'most people didn't report it' are both accurate. The label also supports the other claims: fatigue and stomach side effects are among the most common reactions (≥5%), side effects can lead to fluid loss, and hypoglycemia risk is higher with a sulfonylurea (10.3% vs 2.1%). The NHS tiredness page supports blood tests for anaemia, and the NHS self-help page supports dehydration and irregular eating as causes of tiredness. The safety lines are all present: don't stop or change your medicines, 'Not personal advice', and the prescriber line. Nothing nudges toward eating less. The hook pays off. The fixes: (1) correct the source years (label 2026, NHS pages 2023); (2) in s6, add a 'get medical help' option, because the label pairs fainting or dizziness with possible serious allergic reactions; (3) optionally tidy the awkward hedge in s4. I couldn't read the Lilly PDFs themselves (they came back as binary), but they did download, so the links work. All label numbers were checked against the readable DailyMed copy of the label.

issues.claim: src1 year 2025; src2 year 2024; src3 year 2024
issues.problem: The current Zepbound label on DailyMed was revised on 28 August 2026. The NHS 'Self-help tips to fight tiredness' page was last reviewed on 8 November 2023, and the NHS 'Tiredness and fatigue' page on 2 June 2023. None of these is 2024 or 2025.
issues.fix: Set src1 year to "2026", src2 year to "2023" and src3 year to "2023". If src4 (the Medication Guide) was revised along with the label, set it to "2026" as well.

issues.claim: Dizziness, fainting, or vomiting that won't stop? Contact your prescriber right away.
issues.problem: This is a sensible red-flag line, and it's our own safety tip rather than a quote from the label. But the label and Medication Guide pair fainting or dizziness with possible serious allergic reactions, and for those the advice is to get medical help right away, not just to contact the prescriber. Pointing only to the prescriber could delay urgent care.
issues.fix: Narration: "Stomach side effects are the most common, and vomiting or diarrhea can drain fluids. Dizziness, fainting, or vomiting that won't stop? Contact your prescriber or get medical help right away." On-screen text: "Dizzy or fainting? Get help right away"

issues.problem: The hedge is honest, but it sounds clipped when spoken and may confuse viewers. This is wording polish only; the claim itself is accurate.
issues.fix: Narration: "Eating much less than usual, or not drinking enough, can leave you tired. It may not be the whole story, but it's worth checking."

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the -12/-15 window under speech, so I pulled the overall bed down ~2dB (0.8x) mainly to tame the -8.2dB pause swell and because this piece covers side effects and a "get help right away" safety beat, where the playbook wants music kept low and SFX thinned. Cleaned up a batch of simultaneous duplicate SFX (whoosh/swoosh/tick/bubble/blip layered on the same beat under "Red blood cells," "Stomach," "Not personal advice," and the two brand shots) that were adding clutter without adding anything audible, and dropped two cues that were already essentially inaudible (-39.6dB, -49.3dB, -34.8dB) as mix glitches. Boosted the stat-reveal "ding" (5–7% vs 3%) slightly so the key number gets a felt accent, and nudged up one buried "pop" that had sunk to -21dB. Added two small custom cues — a weary exhale under "Energy drains" and a soft low heartbeat under "Get help right away" — to carry emotional weight without raising volume on a serious safety line.
